newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs caution against too much NATO glee.
newsitem.headline: Czechs caution against too much NATO glee.

text.p: Prague commentators on Wednesday generally welcomed NATO's invitation to the Czech Republic but cautioned against too much glee, saying more attention needed to be paid to the responsibilities of membership.

The largest Czech daily, Mlada Fronta Dnes, contrasting television's primary attention to the worst flooding in the country in a century, topped its edition with the broad headline "NATO Opens Gates for the Czech Republic".
A large frontpage feature cautioned, "In the Alliance We Must Think About the World Around Us".
It said that the invitation did not mean only security guarantees from strong allies but "our own greater share in the defence of world security"

Still, it quoted former prime minister Petr Pithart, a one-time dissident who is now chairman of the Czech Senate as saying: "This is a great day for Czech history, the young Czech Republic and mainly for us, the often-tested Czech people."
Czechs remained split in their support for NATO membership after four decades of Soviet domination.

The government and largest opposition party all have supported NATO membership, but the top opposition Social Democrats have been unsuccesful in pushing through a referendum which they said would provide a healthy debate about NATO.
Mlada Fronta commentator Michal Mocek took a pragmatic look at membership in an editorial leader entitled "NATO Invitation is a Call to Action".
"With the invitation of the West in the pocket, Prague can allow only a few bottles of champagne -- certainly it cannot rest on its laurels," Mocek said.
He said that "NATO is not a political club but a military alliance", and he cited analysts who said that the state of the Czech army lay behind Romania's.
"This all must be overcome on the Czechs' way into the alliance," he said.
Billions of crowns and much attention still must be paid "to creating forces capable and willing to defend itself and help other," Mocek added.

The largest tabloid, Blesk, relegated the invitation behind the floods to page two where it proclaimed: "Czechs, Hungarians, and Poles - NATO Summit Decides after Stormy Debate on Expanding the Pact."
In the left-leaning Pravo, once the former communist party organ Rude Pravo, Josef Vesely asked: "Who Needs NATO, and for What?", but then backed the idea.

"Seemingly illogically, now more than ever since the April 4, 1949 Washington Treaty was signed, countries need a properly functioning military/political organisation of this type." He agreed with those who feared the unknown if NATO had not existed.
